content.title: About
content.content: Parmesan is a hard, aged cheese from Italy made from cow’s milk. It is traditionally aged 12–36 months, developing a granular texture and a nutty, fruity, and buttery flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Parmesan holds a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) status – it can only be produced in specific Italian regions.
Grated Parmesan is a staple topping in cuisines worldwide.
Traditional Parmesan is made from whole cow’s milk without added cream.
Extra‑aged Parmesan (over 24 months) develops a more crystalline structure and a sharper taste.
In Italy, Parmesan is sometimes served as “parmesan balls” – small dough balls coated with grated cheese.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Parmesan provides about 1,100 mg of calcium per 100 g, supporting bone and tooth health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: It contains roughly 35 g of protein per 100 g, aiding muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nerve function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: Fermentation introduces beneficial bacteria that can support gut microbiota.

items.title: Low in lactose
items.content: Long aging breaks down most lactose, making Parmesan often tolerable for those with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may react to Parmesan.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Parmesan contains about 650 mg of sodium per 30 g serving, so those with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: At roughly 430 kcal per 100 g, it should be consumed in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Parmesan is typically grated over pasta, risotto, soups, and salads. It can also be served in small shards as a snack, paired with fruit, nuts, or honey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Parmesan in its original packaging or wrapped in parchment paper and then a loose‑fit plastic bag in the refrigerator at 4–7 °C. For longer storage, it can be frozen wrapped in foil, though texture may change.

chicken-or-turkey-breaded-fried-garden-s.title: Breaded Fried Chicken or Turkey with Garden Salad and Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of pieces of chicken or turkey breast coated in breadcrumbs and deep‑fried until golden and crispy. It is served with a garden salad made of lettuce or other leafy greens, tomato, carrot, cheese and optional additional vegetables. No dressing is added.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey are among the most popular sources of lean protein.
Frying in a breadcrumb coating creates a crunchy crust that locks in the meat’s juices.
Cheese adds calcium and a creamy flavor to the salad.
A salad without dressing preserves the natural taste of fresh vegetables and reduces added fats.
The combination of protein, vegetables, and dairy makes the meal nutritionally balanced.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide all essential amino acids, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: White meat contains less saturated fat than red meat, which is beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat is high in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus from cheese
items.content: Cheese supplies calcium and phosphorus, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Fiber and antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Tomatoes, carrots, and leafy greens provide dietary fiber, vitamins A, C and various antioxidants.

items.title: Allergy to poultry or dairy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken, turkey or cheese.

items.title: High sodium in cheese
items.content: Cheeses often contain salt; people monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt varieties.

items.title: Trans fats from frying
items.content: Repeated deep‑frying can generate trans fats; using high‑smoke‑point oils is recommended.

items.title: Risk of undercooking
items.content: Insufficiently cooked poultry may harbor harmful bacteria; ensure an internal temperature of 75 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The fried pieces can be eaten on their own, added to sandwiches, wraps or salads. Serve the garden salad as a side: toss the vegetables, sprinkle grated cheese, and place the crispy chicken or turkey alongside.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared dish in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for up to 2 days. Keep the vegetables in a separate airtight container and the fried meat in its own container to maintain crispness.

chicken-or-turkey-noodles-and-vegetables.title: Chicken or turkey with noodles and vegetables (no carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens), no sauce

content.title: About
content.content: This dish combines tender chicken or turkey meat, boiled noodles, and a mix of vegetables, excluding carrots, broccoli, and dark‑green leafy greens. It is prepared without any sauce, making it a light and nutritious option for those watching fat and sugar intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey are excellent sources of lean protein.
Noodles made from durum wheat provide lasting satiety.
Vegetables such as bell pepper, zucchini, and mushrooms add vitamins and minerals without many calories.
The lack of sauce lets you taste the natural flavors of the ingredients.
The dish can be easily adapted to different cuisines by changing herbs and spices.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey contain all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Lean meat and the absence of sauce make the meal suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Provides complex carbohydrates
items.content: Noodles supply a steady release of glucose, supporting sustained energy.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from vegetables
items.content: Bell pepper, zucchini, and mushrooms are high in vitamin C, vitamin B6, potassium, and magnesium.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Without heavy sauces and with moderate fiber, the dish is easy on the digestive system.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken or turkey proteins.

items.title: Gluten in noodles
items.content: Standard wheat noodles contain gluten; those with celiac disease should choose gluten‑free alternatives.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If pre‑flavored noodles are used, sodium levels may be higher than expected.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Meat must be fully cooked to avoid risks of salmonella or campylobacter infection.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot; garnish with fresh herbs (parsley, dill) or a squeeze of lemon juice for extra aroma. A sprinkle of seeds (pumpkin, sunflower) can add a pleasant crunch if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. When reheating, add a splash of water to keep the noodles from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Barley soup is a traditional dish made from whole barley grains, vegetables, and sometimes meat. Barley gives the soup a thick, slightly nutty texture and a rich aroma. The dish is popular in Eastern European and Asian cuisines, where barley is valued for its nourishment and warming properties.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Barley is one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown for over 10,000 years.
In Russian cuisine barley soup is often called “rassolnik” when pickles are added.
Barley contains beta‑glucans that help lower cholesterol levels.
The Japanese version of barley soup, called “mizuho,” is often served with seaweed.
Barley readily absorbs flavors, making the soup versatile with herbs and spices.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Barley provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Barley contains thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Barley supplies magnesium, phosphorus, iron, and zinc, important for bones and immune function.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Beta‑glucans help reduce LDL (bad) cholesterol.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Antioxidants and trace elements in barley help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Cereal allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to barley.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Barley contains gluten, so it should be avoided by people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High carbohydrate load
items.content: Portion control is advisable for those monitoring blood sugar levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Barley soup is served hot, often enriched with fresh vegetables, herbs, and pieces of chicken or beef. Adding potatoes, carrots, and onions creates a heartier flavor. Soaking the barley beforehand can reduce cooking time.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked soup in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions; the texture may become slightly thinner after thawing, which can be corrected by adding a little water.
